Ironing Board surfing Charles had been looking forward to his summer vacation with his family. He was excited to go to the beach. His parents finally agreed to let his best friend Henry come along. Henry and Charles had been practicing their surfing on his mom's ironing board.

Despite the broken hinges and the goose egg on Henry's head, practicing had gone well. The six-hour drive to the beach passed quickly, as Charles and Henry had video game competitions. They finally arrived at the beach and set up camp that night. Henry and Charles could hardly sleep. As the sun was peeking over the hills, the boys were trotting down the beach to catch some waves. As they paddled through the water and turned to catch a wave, they quickly learned that their ironing-board training was inadequate for the strength of the ocean.

In their focus and concentration, the boys lost track of time. They decided to head in for lunch. Fighting the waves, they finally made it to shore. As they walked across the sand, they found themselves on strange beach they did not recognize. Charles' parents were nowhere in sight. There wasn't a single person on the beach.

"Whoa!" exclaimed Henry.

"What are we going to do?" moaned Charles.

The Cloud Who Kept Her Rain
High above the plains floated a cloud named Nimbus. She was the biggest, fluffiest cloud in the sky, and she was very proud of it.
'If I let my rain fall, I will shrink,' she thought. 'Then nobody will admire me.' So she held on to every drop.
Down below, the grass turned brown and crisp. The creek shrank to a muddy trickle. The farmers looked up at Nimbus and sighed.
A little wind tugged at her edge. 'The land is thirsty,' it whispered. 'Your rain is not yours to keep.'
Nimbus puffed herself up even more. But her heavy load made her grumpy and grey, and soon nobody admired her at all.
At last, with a great rumble, she let go. Rain poured onto the fields. The creek gurgled back to life, and the grass turned green.
Nimbus was thin and pale now, but the farmers waved and children danced in the puddles. For the first time, Nimbus felt truly light.
QuestionText: Why did Nimbus hold on to her rain?
AnswerA: She was afraid she would shrink.
AnswerB: She was waiting for the wind.
AnswerC: She wanted the creek to dry up.
AnswerD: She was too high above the plains.

The Platypus Man
David Fleay was born in Victoria in 1907. Even as a boy, he loved Australian animals. He kept lizards, possums and birds, and spent hours watching them.
When he grew up, David became a teacher, and later a wildlife keeper. At Healesville Sanctuary, he set himself a very difficult goal. No one had ever bred a platypus in a zoo. Platypuses are shy, and they need clean water and lots of food each day.
David built a special home for them, with a pond and a winding burrow. He fed his pair of platypuses, Jack and Jill, hundreds of worms and yabbies. Then, in 1943, something amazing happened. A baby platypus was born! It was named Corrie, and it was the first platypus ever bred in captivity.
Later, David moved to Queensland and opened his own wildlife park. He worked hard to protect animals and to teach people about them. Today, the park still carries his name.
QuestionText: What was the name of the baby platypus?
AnswerA: Jack
AnswerB: Jill
AnswerC: Corrie
AnswerD: Healesville

The Box from 2025
In the year 2125, the students of Bayside School gathered in the hall. A rusty metal box sat on the stage. It had been buried under the school garden one hundred years before.
Principal Ngo lifted the creaky lid. Clunk! Out came a pile of strange objects.
First was a small metal key. 'What is it for?' asked Mia. In her time, every door simply opened when it saw your face.
Next came a folded sheet of paper covered in coloured lines and the names of streets. Leo turned it around and around. 'Maybe it's a picture of spaghetti,' he said. Everyone giggled.
At the bottom was a letter written in wobbly pencil by a girl named Ruby. 'Hello, future kids!' it began. 'I hope you still play outside and eat ice cream. Please tell me if there are flying cars!'
Mia smiled. She looked out the window at the sky, where cars hummed past like bees. 'Let's write back,' she said. 'We'll put our letter in the box for 2225.'

AnswerA: under the school hall
AnswerB: beneath the stage
AnswerC: beside the front gate
AnswerD: under the school garden

The Toast Mystery
Have you ever dropped a piece of buttered toast? If you have, it probably landed butter side down, making a sticky mess on the floor. Many people think this is just bad luck, but scientists say there is a simple reason.
When toast slides off a plate or the edge of a table, it starts to spin as it falls. A kitchen table is not very high, so the toast only has time to make about half a turn before it hits the floor. The toast started with the butter facing up, so half a turn flips it over and the butter faces down. Splat!
Some people have tested this by dropping toast again and again. It landed butter side down much more often than butter side up.
If tables were much taller, the toast would have time to spin all the way round. But nobody wants a table taller than a grown-up!
So how can you save your snack? The best plan is to hold your plate carefully with both hands. Or you could just eat your toast quickly!
